subtype: Approach: pause and take a break when emotions rise [Revision]
passage:
"That's not what happened, Papa, and you know it," Nandini said, louder than she meant to. Her heart was hammering.

Kamal put down his glass. "Don't raise your voice at me."

"I'm sorry. Look, this matters to me, that's why I'm shouting. But I can feel myself getting angry, and I don't want us to have a bad evening."

"So what do you want, to stop?"

"Not stop. Pause. Can we carry on after tea?"

He frowned. "Fine. Fifteen minutes."

"Thanks, Papa."

She stepped out on the balcony, breathed slowly, and watched the traffic lights go green and red until her hands stopped shaking. When the kettle whistled, she went back in.

qa.q: What did Nandini suggest they do after tea?
qa.a: She suggested carrying on after tea.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when she stepped onto the balcony?
qa.a: Nandini was angry and shaken, with a racing heart and trembling hands, but she wanted to calm down and protect the evening.

qa.q: What could Nandini and her father try when they resume, and why?
qa.a: They could take turns speaking without interrupting, and Nandini could say the point that matters most, because the break is only useful if the talk stays calmer.

qa.q: How might Kamal see being asked to pause instead of being shouted at?
qa.a: Kamal may feel a bit stung but also respected, since Nandini named her own anger and offered a way to continue.

grounding: Noticing a raised voice and racing heart, the student says the topic matters, proposes continuing after tea, and steps outside.

subtype: Approach: pause and take a break when emotions rise [Revision]
passage:
I'm Vijay. Last Sunday my Nandini Masi and I got into it about the new rules for street vendors. She thinks they'll clean up the market; I think they'll push people like the woman who sells us vegetables out of work.
Five minutes in, I heard my own voice. It was loud, louder than I talk to anyone. My heart was going fast and my face was hot. Masi's voice was rising too, and my little cousins had gone quiet.
Last time that happened, we didn't speak for a month.
So I stopped. I said, 'Masi, this matters to me, and I think it matters to you. But I'm getting too heated to listen properly. Can we talk about it again after tea?' Then I went and stood on the balcony for ten minutes, breathing, watching the street.
After tea we did talk, more calmly. We still disagreed. But she said she'd never thought about the vegetable seller, and I admitted the market really is a mess. Nobody stormed off.

qa.q: What was the disagreement between Vijay and Masi about?
qa.a: The new rules for street vendors.

qa.q: What signs told Vijay that emotions were rising?
qa.a: A loud voice, a racing heart and a hot face, which Vijay noticed as anger building before it went too far.
It showed the topic mattered while giving both time to calm down, so they could listen instead of fight.

qa.q: How might the little cousins have felt?
qa.a: Uneasy and quiet as voices rose, then likely relieved when the argument paused and nobody stormed off.

grounding: Shows a young person noticing a raised voice and racing heart in a political argument, naming that the topic matters and pausing until after tea.

subtype: Approach: pause and take a break when emotions rise [Revision]
passage:
Written after the wedding lunch, 18 February. Vidya, Sumit's aunt.
I want to note this because I was proud of Sumit today, and I don't say that enough.
At the table, Papa started on the new crop-price rules and the government, as he always does, and Sumit disagreed. Within minutes they were both loud. I saw Sumit's hand go to his chest and his face turn red. The relatives nearby had stopped eating.
Then Sumit took a breath and said, 'Dadu, I care about this, and so do you. But my heart is racing and I'm not listening well. Can we pick it up after tea?' He pushed his chair back and went out to the garden. Papa grumbled, but let him go.
Twenty minutes later I saw them together near the tea counter, talking at a normal volume. Papa even laughed once.
Last Diwali they didn't speak for weeks after a fight like this. Today a pause did what an hour of arguing never has.

qa.q: Where did Sumit go when he paused?
What does Sumit's hand going to his chest suggest?
qa.a: His heart was racing; he felt heated and noticed his anger rising before it took over.

qa.q: What else could Sumit do if the topic comes up again?
qa.a: Name the signs early, suggest a break in the same way, and return to it when both are calm.

qa.q: How does the lunch look to Vidya, who wrote the note?
qa.a: Vidya is proud to see Sumit pause instead of fight, and relieved it did not turn into weeks of silence.

grounding: Shows a young person noticing rising anger in a political argument with a grandfather, pausing for tea and returning calmly.
